paper_title: DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Evaluation has been central to advances in AI, and it is equally critical to autonomous discovery. Yet scaling autonomous discovery to real-world engineering challenges faces a fundamental bottleneck: the cost of evaluating progress. In real settings, a single true evaluation, such as a full benchmark or serving trace, can take hours, so a search can afford only a handful of true evaluations. We present DuoDiscover, a search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress efficiently, through three mechanisms. First, each worker in a fleet of coding agents co-discovers an optimization target and a fast, tailored proxy evaluator, which we call a yardstick. The agent then hill-climbs the yardstick rather than the true evaluation. Second, since search can exploit gaps between a yardstick and the true objective, fidelity tests continually recheck each yardstick's ranking and invalidate any that drift. Third, the fleet is bottom-up, with no central decomposition of the problem. A lightweight orchestrator spawns and terminates agents, briefs running ones, and seeds new agents with others' confirmed work. DuoDiscover enables autonomous optimization from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate DuoDiscover on two repository-level benchmarks and four GPU and TPU kernel suites covering hundreds of kernels. On SWE-fficiency, it doubles the average speedup of human experts. On SOL-Exec, it ranks first on 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three on 212. On the heavily optimized vLLM and SQLite engines, DuoDiscover achieves 1.92$\times$ and 1.38$\times$ gains over the base code. On a CPU microarchitecture optimization task with evaluations of up to 28 hours, DuoDiscover surpasses both AlphaEvolve-based ArchAgent v2 and the best human design, with 1.65$\times$ ArchAgent v2's gain in 16.7 days versus more than 40 days, advancing the frontier of autonomous chip design.

Introduction Search-based discovery systems that couple large language models (LLMs) with iterative search and evaluator feedback have achieved strong results across mathematics (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), algorithms (Novikov et al., 2025), and systems optimization (Cheng et al., 2025). Evaluation has long driven progress in AI, yet most prior work on autonomous discovery focuses on refining the search harness itself (Cemri et al., 2026; Lange et al., 2026), largely treating the evaluator as given and fixed. On real engineering systems, however, that assumption breaks down: evaluating progress becomes the bottleneck. For instance, optimizing vLLM for multi-objective serving requires 85 minutes per true evaluation, limiting even frontier coding agents to dozen evaluations within 20-hour search budget. Overcoming this bottleneck is key to scaling autonomous discovery across science and real-world engineering. natural solution is to guide search with cheap proxy evaluators instead of expensive true evaluations. This works because large speedups often come from focused edits to few small regions of code, which we call targets, whose progress can be measured much more cheaply than the entire true evaluation. However, proxy evaluators are usually target-specific, making it impractical to design one by hand for every target. Moreover, effective proxy-guided search requires jointly identifying promising targets and cheap, faithful proxies: optimizing the wrong target yields little benefit, while an inaccurate proxy can misguide search. Even faithful proxies can become unreliable as search exploits discrepancies between the proxy and the true objective, improving proxy scores without real gains. We propose DuoDiscover, search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress when evaluation becomes the bottleneck. Each worker agent co-discovers promising optimization target and cheap proxy evaluator, called yardstick, then hill-climbs on the yardstick to find better solutions. Beyond co-discovery, DuoDiscover addresses two further challenges. The first is maintaining evaluation fidelity. yardstick that initially ranks edits like the true objective can drift as the agent adapts to it. DuoDiscover continually runs fidelity tests to invalidate drifting yardsticks and requires true evaluation to confirm every gain before it is accepted. The second is target selection, choosing which regions to optimize among many candidate targets with unpredictable payoffs. Rather than decomposing the problem centrally, DuoDiscover deploys bottom-up fleet of independent worker agents for co-discovery. Because worker agents are cheap but true evaluations are expensive, lightweight orchestrator manages only the true evaluations: it steers them toward agents making progress, terminates stalled agents, and combines compatible gains. DuoDiscover delivers autonomous optimization at every level of the computing stack, from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate it on two repository benchmarks, four GPU/TPU kernel suites, and real-world systems. On repositories, DuoDiscover doubles the human-expert speedup on SWE-fficiency and beats all baselines on FormulaCode, by 21% over the strongest. For GPU kernels, DuoDiscover achieves 14% higher speed-of-light (SOL) score than the best baseline, ranking first on SOL-Exec for 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three for 212 at the time of submission. On speedup over optimized Pallas kernels, ahead TPU-Inference kernels, DuoDiscover attains 2.68 speedup over XLA. On of the best baseline at 2.38 speedup. We evaluate DuoDiscover on tasks across two repository optimization benchmarks (FormulaCode and SWE-fficiency; Ma et al., 2025; Sehgal et al., 2026) and four GPU and TPU kernel suites (SOL-Exec, JAXBench, TPU-Inference, and FA4; Chen et al., 2026a; Lin et al., 2026a; Tschand et al., 2026; vLLM Project, 2025). Each task requires speeding up the source code while maintaining functional correctness. Unlike algorithmic benchmarks (Novikov et al., 2025), where evaluation finishes in seconds, single true evaluation here can take minutes to hours  (Table 8)  . Scoring. All methods are evaluated under the same wall-clock time and number of agents. Repositories are scored by end-to-end execution speedup while checking for correctness. Kernels are scored by speedup over reference code or as percentage of theoretical peak hardware throughput (speed-of-light or SOL score; Lin et al., 2026a). The reported score of run is the median of several re-evaluations of its final candidate, chosen by lower confidence bound, with Student-𝑡 interval. The best score seen during the run is never reported, and candidate that fails the correctness check is reported as no result. Search statistics and the analyses of 4 use stratified sample of 20 SWE-fficiency tasks and 50 SOL-Exec kernels that covers every task type and evaluation time. Baselines. We compare DuoDiscover against agentic (Claude Code; Anthropic, 2025), evolutionary (OpenEvolve; Sharma, 2025; its agentic variant on the repository benchmarks), and domain-specific baselines, namely AVO (Chen et al., 2026a), KDA (Zou et al., 2026), and profiler-guided approach modeled on PerfAgent (Deng et al., 2026) (Appendix B.2). Related work In this section, we describe three lines of related research: LLM-driven coding and discovery agents, LLM-generated tests and evaluators, and multi-fidelity optimization methods. Coding and discovery agents. LLMs are increasingly used as operators for search and optimization, transforming automated code generation into an engine for scientific and algorithmic discovery. FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) was among the first methods of this kind and found new best-known constructions for combinatorics problems. AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) scaled this into an autonomous pipeline that evolves population of programs from programmatic feedback. Subsequent work has extended this evolutionary approach along several axes: improving efficiency (Jiang et al., 2026; Lange et al., 2026), dynamically adapting mutation strategies (Cemri et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), optimizing the model weights with test-time reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026b; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026), and overcoming local minima (Yan et al., 2026). Discovery agents have been proposed for variety of tasks, including repository-level runtime optimization (Deng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026b), low-level kernel acceleration (Chen et al., 2026a; Dai et al., 2026; Liao et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Wei et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2026), and computer 10 DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck architecture discovery (Blasberg et al., 2026; Gonzalez et al., 2026; Gupta et al., 2026). For some tasks, the cost of evaluations can be major bottleneck for optimization. To mitigate this bottleneck, SIFT (Fu et al., 2026) uses the expensive evaluations only for the most promising solutions. While prior methods like AlphaEvolve allow users to specify cheaper checks ahead of the full evaluation, DuoDiscover is the first discovery agent that finds both the solution and cheap evaluators which are validated or invalidated during the discovery process. LLM-generated tests and evaluators. Prior work has also used LLMs to synthesize test cases and evaluators to guide code search. Generated unit tests are used to rank candidate implementations (Chen et al., 2023) and to drive iterative refinement (Chen et al., 2024; Ehrlich et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2025; Shinn et al., 2023). Alternatively, ExecCritic (Tao et al., 2026) freezes generated tests before changing the implementation so unverified checks cannot misguide revisions (Chen et al., 2026b). While these works use LLMs and coding agents to construct software correctness tests, DuoDiscover extends this idea beyond correctness testing to discover cheap, target-specific yardsticks for fast optimization. Multi-fidelity optimization (MFO). MFO methods balance cheap, approximate evaluations and expensive, accurate ones by spending most of the budget on low-cost proxy and querying the expensive objective sparingly (Li and Li, 2026). There are two common approaches. The first is to fit cheap surrogate model that predicts the objective and is corrected as real measurements arrive (Chen et al., 2018; Fernández-Godino et al., 2019; Forrester et al., 2007; Kandasamy et al., 2016; Kennedy and OHagan, 2000). The second is adaptive resource allocation, which evaluates many candidates cheaply, then progressively concentrates budget on the promising ones and discards the rest (Falkner et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018). Uniquely, our method uses agents to synthesize cheap proxy evaluators and validate or invalidate them during search. 6. Conclusion Scaling autonomous discovery requires not only finding better solutions, but also discovering how to evaluate them efficiently. In this work, we have argued that search in this regime must discover both what to optimize (target) and cheaper way to measure progress on it (yardstick). We present DuoDiscover, bottom-up search system that builds on this idea for evaluation-bottlenecked settings. Across two repository benchmarks, four kernel suites, and five real-world case studies, DuoDiscover demonstrates autonomous optimization across the computing stack, from software to chip architecture. More broadly, co-discovery, enabling agents to find their own targets and yardsticks, opens path toward scaling autonomous discovery across science and engineering. Limitations. While DuoDiscover accelerates optimization across diverse domains, it has two primary limitations. First, when no faithful yardstick can be constructed for target, DuoDiscover falls back to standard search over the expensive true objective. Second, constructing yardsticks and running initial fidelity tests incurs an upfront warmup overhead, making DuoDiscover less advantageous under extremely short evaluation budgets.
